object.name: Pillar of Fire
object.subtitle: Theophanic column of flame in which God appears to prophets and protects his servants
object.aliases: pillar of fire, cloud of darkness
object.description:
The pillar of fire is the Book of Mormon’s primary image of theophany, the visible glory in which God reveals himself directly to mortals. It opens the entire narrative: when Lehi pleads in behalf of Jerusalem, “there came a pillar of fire and dwelt upon a rock before him; and he saw and heard much; and because of the things which he saw and heard he did quake and tremble exceedingly” (1 Nephi 1:6). The image deliberately echoes the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt, marking Lehi at the outset as a new Mosaic figure called to lead a remnant out of a doomed city.

The motif returns in the most arresting prison scene in the record. Nephi and Lehi, sons of Helaman, are cast into the prison of the land of Nephi by an unbelieving Lamanite multitude, but the brothers are “encircled about as if by fire, even insomuch that they durst not lay their hands upon them for fear lest they should be burned.” The flame does not consume the prophets but instead becomes the medium of their preaching, and when the cloud of darkness around the multitude finally disperses, they themselves stand encircled by the same protective fire (Helaman 5:23-24, 5:43-44). What had been a sign of judgment in Egypt becomes here a sign of grace.

At Bountiful the pattern peaks. Following the prayer of the disciples, the multitude beholds the children encircled “as if it were by fire,” with angels ministering to them out of heaven (3 Nephi 19:14). Across these episodes the pillar of fire functions both vertically and horizontally: it descends to mark a prophet, and it surrounds to shelter a community. Wherever it appears, it announces that the same God who spoke from Sinai is present, sanctifying ground, sealing testimony, and consuming nothing but unbelief.

object.name: Interpreters
object.subtitle: Two stones fastened in a bow by which seers translate sealed records
object.description:
The interpreters, called in later revelation the Urim and Thummim, are a pair of clear stones “fastened into the two rims of a bow” (Mosiah 28:13) prepared from the foundation of the world for the translation of sacred records. King Limhi first seeks news of his people’s lost prophet, and Ammon tells him of a man in Zarahemla “that can translate the records; for he has wherewith that he can look, and translate all records that are of ancient date; and it is a gift from God” (Mosiah 8:13). Limhi rejoices, knowing the twenty-four plates recovered from the Jaredite ruin can now be opened: “a great mystery is contained within these plates, and these interpreters were doubtless prepared for the purpose of unfolding all such mysteries” (Mosiah 8:19).

Their origin lies with the brother of Jared. After he sees the finger of the Lord, he is told, “these two stones will I give unto thee, and ye shall seal them up also with the things which ye shall write,” so that in due time they may “magnify to the eyes of men these things which ye shall write” (Ether 3:23-24). Moroni later confirms that the Lord commanded him to “seal up the interpretation thereof” with the record itself (Ether 4:5). In the Nephite line they pass from Mosiah to Alma (Mosiah 28:20) and across generations as one of the sacred regalia of the seer, alongside the brass plates, sword of Laban, and Liahona.

Alma instructs Helaman that “these interpreters were prepared that the word of God might be fulfilled” (Alma 37:24), making the stones a guarantor of revelation across time. They embody the Book of Mormon’s theology of seership, in which prophetic vision is mediated through humble physical means and confined to those called and prepared. To possess them is not to wield magic but to bear a charge: God’s hidden words will be made plain only at his appointed hour.

object.name: Riplakish's Prisons
object.subtitle: Jaredite forced-labor prisons built by king Riplakish to enforce taxes and refine fine gold
object.description: Riplakish's prisons were a network of Jaredite forced-labor camps built under the reign of king Riplakish to enforce his tax regime and feed the royal workshops. The record reports that he “did build many prisons, and whoso would not be subject unto taxes he did cast into prison; and whoso was not able to pay taxes he did cast into prison; and he did cause that they should labor continually for their support; and whoso refused to labor he did cause to be put to death” (Ether 10:6). The economic logic of the system is recorded in the next verse: “he did obtain all his fine work, yea, even his fine gold he did cause to be refined in prison; and all manner of fine workmanship he did cause to be wrought in prison” (Ether 10:7). The prisons functioned simultaneously as debtors' jails, conscript workhouses, and royal smelters — the only sustained example in the Book of Mormon of incarceration as a state industry. After forty-two years the people rose against Riplakish and slew him, driving his descendants out of the land and ending the regime that the prisons sustained.

object.name: Horn
object.subtitle: Biblical emblem of strength, dominion, and covenant might promised to Israel
object.description:
The horn appears in the Book of Mormon almost entirely as a borrowed biblical idiom of strength rather than as a physical object on the Nephite landscape. Its most prominent occurrence is in the risen Lord’s sermon at Bountiful, where he applies the language of Micah to the gathering of his covenant people: “I will make my people with whom the Father hath covenanted, yea, I will make thy horn iron, and I will make thy hoofs brass. And thou shalt beat in pieces many people; and I will consecrate their gain unto the Lord” (3 Nephi 20:19). The image is drawn from ancient Near Eastern royal iconography in which the horn of an animal symbolizes irresistible power, often associated with the bull or ox as a sign of kingship.

For the risen Christ to assign Israel an “iron horn” is to reverse the diaspora narrative of weakness and scattering. The covenant remnant, long gored by the horns of empire, becomes itself the instrument by which the proud are thrown down and the wealth of the nations is consecrated to the Lord. The metallic registers (iron, brass) link the prophecy with other Book of Mormon images of indestructibility, including the rod of iron of Lehi’s dream and the brazen plates that carry the law into the new world.

While the horn does not function in Lehite narrative as a literal cultic object such as the altar horns of Israelite worship, its symbolic weight is heavy. It declares that the apparent weakness of Christ’s covenant people is provisional, that their final posture is not victimhood but eschatological triumph, and that the gathering of Israel is also the assembling of a force the world cannot withstand.
